title: Diagnostic Questions: Is There Value in Just One? tonmaths.com/resourcesnew/8.%20Research/Formative%20Assessment/Is%20there%20value%20in %20just%20one%20-%20Dylan%20Wiliam%202006.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), September 24, 2025 — original paper: https://mrbar
summary: Barton's summary covers a paper contrasting two models of data-driven instruction: a 'data-push' model where teachers receive periodic test results, and a 'decision-pull' model — exemplified by the DIMS project — where teachers use single, well-designed questions to make immediate instructional decisions. The paper argues that although one question is less reliable than a full test, its value for real-time classroom adjustment outweighs that limitation, particularly when judging a whole class rather than an individual. It sets out what makes a good decision-pull question: it must be quick to administer to every student, and its wrong answers must be interpretable — tied to genuine misconceptions rather than random distractors. The authors argue for selecting a small set of questions that give strong coverage of the domain being taught, so assessment becomes something integrated into instruction rather than bolted onto the end of it. A recurring theme is that data is worthless if teachers can't or don't act on it — collecting information without using it can leave students worse off than not collecting it at all.
points: The 'decision-pull' model — single, high-quality questions used to make instant teaching decisions — is framed as more useful in the classroom than the 'data-push' model of periodic large-scale test data.
Good decision-pull questions must have interpretable wrong answers: distractors tied to common misconceptions, not vague or arbitrary options.
Even though a single question is statistically less reliable than a full test, a well-chosen single item still beats making instructional decisions with no data at all.
Teachers who collect assessment data but don't use it get worse outcomes than teachers who never collected it in the first place — assessment only has value when integrated with instruction.
quotes: Teachers can use single, high-quality questions to make quick decisions about what students understand and to adjust their teaching to meet students' learning needs.

This is called a “decision-pull” approach to data-driven instruction, and it contrasts with the “data-push” approach where teachers are given large amounts of data that they may not have time to use or may not find helpful.

In addition to being easy to collect, good decision-pull questions should also have incorrect answers that help teachers understand what students do not understand and provide ideas about what to do about it.

While the reliability of a single question is lower than the reliability of a test with multiple questions, a single question can still provide enough information to guide instruction in real-time, especially if the question is well-chosen.
Teachers who collect information about student achievement but are unable to do anything with that information get worse results than teachers who do not collect such information at all.
While the accuracy of a decision based on a single item may be far from perfect, it is better than a decision based on no data at all.
